Why use a feature branch for a database change?
column2:
To isolate work until it is ready for review and integration.
A feature branch keeps work in progress off main. Use a pull request when the change is ready so the team can review and build it before merging.
Review source

column1: In a feature-branch workflow, what state must main maintain?
column2:
It must remain deployable.
A deployable main lets the team release from a known branch without first removing incomplete changes. Required reviews and build checks reduce the chance of invalid schema reaching it.
Review source

column1: Why keep database feature branches short-lived?
column2:
To reduce divergence and the difficulty of merging changes.
The longer the branch stays open, the more changes main can accumulate without it. Integrate small, reviewed changes promptly so there are fewer competing edits to reconcile.
Review source

column1: Why open a pull request before merging SQL project changes into main?
column2:
Review and validate proposed changes before merging them into main.
A pull request exposes the proposed SQL diff and build results before the change enters main. Reviewers can ask for fixes while the change is still isolated on its branch.
Review source

column1: When you change a column's type or size, what compatibility risk must SQL pull request reviewers look for?
column2:
Existing queries or stored procedures can depend on its old definition.
A definition can compile while older consumers still rely on its previous contract. For example, narrowing a column can break an application write that supplies a longer value.
Review source

column1: A SQL pull request drops a populated column. What must reviewers assess before approving it?
column2:
Possible data loss and any required data migration.
Review the change against real target data, not only the model. For example, dropping a populated column can require copying or transforming its values before the column is removed.
Review source

column1: A pull request adds a required lookup table. Which script must reviewers check for its initial values?
column2:
The corresponding post-deployment reference data scripts.
The changed schema can create or rename a lookup table, but it does not populate that table by itself. Review the post-deployment script that supplies the values the application expects.
Review source

column1: Which GitHub branch-protection setting gates merging on the SQL build check?
column2:
Require status checks to pass before merging.
Select the status check that reports the SQL build on pull requests. A skipped GitHub status check can satisfy the protection rule, so make sure the required job actually builds the project.
Review source

column1: Why can Git need manual help when two branches edit the same CREATE TABLE lines?
column2:
Git cannot automatically reconcile the competing edits.
Git merges text rather than understanding table definitions. If two branches replace the same lines in different ways, Git can need you to choose the intended combined SQL.
Review source

column1: Both branches add a different column to the same CREATE TABLE statement. How do you keep both additions?
column2:
Combine both intended additions into one valid definition and remove the conflict markers.
Keep both column definitions if both changes are wanted. Fix separators and remove the conflict markers before staging the file, then build to make sure the combined definition is valid.
Review source

column1: Git merges the branches without conflicts. Why build the combined SQL project before approving the pull request?
column2:
A clean text merge can still introduce broken references between objects.
Git only establishes that it merged the text. A procedure on one branch can still refer to a column the other branch renamed. Build the merged project to catch broken references.
Review source

column1: Before merging branches, how can you save uncommitted changes so a conflict does not put them at risk?
column2:
Commit or stash the local changes first.
Commit or stash so Git can recover your starting changes separately from the merge. If you enter a merge with uncommitted changes, aborting it cannot always reconstruct the prior state.
Review source

column1: Which Azure Repos branch policy requires a specified number of pull request approvals?
column2:
Require a minimum number of reviewers.
The policy sets the minimum count of approvals required to complete the pull request. Other required conditions, such as a successful build, still need to pass.
Review source

column1: Which Azure Repos reviewer option excludes approval by the person who pushed the latest changes?
column2:
Prohibit the most recent pusher from approving their own changes.
This option prevents the last person to push from counting their own approval toward the requirement. Another eligible reviewer must provide the approval that counts.
Review source

column1: Which Azure Repos option clears earlier approvals on a new push but keeps reject and wait votes?
column2:
Reset all approval votes (does not reset votes to reject or wait).
This setting clears earlier approvals so reviewers can assess the newly pushed version. A rejection or a request to wait stays in place rather than being erased by the push.
Review source

column1: How can Azure Repos require database-team review only for changes under a SQL project path?
column2:
Use an Automatically included reviewers policy set to Required with a matching path filter.
The path filter limits the required reviewer rule to pull requests with matching files. The database team becomes a required reviewer for those changes without gating unrelated paths.
Review source
